Here's the ELI5 for how the mortgage market works for anyone who doesn't know, skip if you want

Banks make loans, we all know that, you probably have a bank within 5 miles of your house (or twenty!). But even the biggest banks have a limit as to the amount of money they can lend. What does a bank do when it has no more money to lend? Instead of shutting down their home lending division after they lend all their money, they sell many of the loans they made to investors on what we call the secondary market. This is done at a profit and has a nice effect of freeing up money to lend to the next group of home buyers.

Sometimes, however the private investors don't want to buy the loans the bank has made, particularly groups of loans with lower income, first time home buyers, or minority areas. So the government in the earlier part of the 20th century created government sponsored enterprises (GSE's) to buy those loans. Think of the GSE's as quasi independent companies that were started by the government, but act as for profit businesses with the caveat that the government could still mandate they do certain things. Fannie Mae for instance can ONLY buy loans on the secondary market. They can't diversify their investments like a normal company can. You could however by shares of a GSE similar to how you could buy Microsoft. Over the last century there has been a yin and yang going on where the private market and the GSE's would spend decades oscillating between one dominating the other. Then the financial collapse happened and the government started taking over many aspects of the mortgage market. /ELI5

Warning: Don't take this as defending all of the banks actions, but the banks have been unfairly attacked by the current administration.

The US government in the late 90's and 2000's forced the banks to expand their lending to include the people most unlikely to pay (read: minorities). If the banks refused they could have lost their access to making FHA Insurable loans, which would have put any bank at a massive competitive disadvantage. So of course, the banks played ball.

The next problem was that even if the banks could be strong armed into lending to non-ideal borrowers, the GSE's like Fannie Mae didn't necessarily WANT to buy these loans (remember they were still operating to make a profit). It took heavy pressure from the government to get the GSE's to buy these non-ideal loans. In short, the government said to the loan originators to lend to the under privileged and then heavily implied to the GSE's that they had a mandate to buy those same loans. The real estate bubble covered up the bad underwriting which was bred from this system and the subsequent crash in 2008 exposed how bad the underwriting had been.

In the fallout the government took every opportunity to insert itself further into the mortgage market.

You heard about the bailouts of the banks most likely. But the biggest change was that the GSE's were brought by the treasury into what we call "conservatorship". This is when the government decided they were "too big to fail" and used its authority to take the GSE's over. This guaranteed the GSE's wouldn't go out of business until the GSE's could get back on their feet, thus the term "conservatorship".

Except, the treasury decided to keep all the profits from the GSE's for itself even after being paid back many times over. Theoretically, there is no way the GSE's could ever leave conservatorship. In a roundabout way, most of the profit from the interest on typical mortgages actually goes to the treasury (which then goes to pay interest on the national debt). If your tin foil hat was firmly affixed to your head you might even think all of this was done by design.

But the government wasn't done yet. They had the GSE's under their control but they still wanted to get a little more money from the banks, because of course more money is always good.

The government dusted off a 100+ year old regulation called the false claims act to use as a major weapon to shake down the banks. This act was originally, and I'm not joking, used to prosecute people who sold lame mules to the US government. The government has been going down the list in the past 10 years of the biggest banks they could find, threatening them with billion dollar fines, but offering to settle for substantially less if the bank didn't put up a fight. The banks are then allowed to admit to no wrong doing and resume business as usual.

Interestingly, the prosecutions have occurred almost in the exact order of the size of the banks. The DOJ didn't have the resources to go after every bank at once, so they pursued the banks one by one which continues to this day. They are currently targeting Guild Mortgage and threatening them with fines that would put them out of business. As usual the gov't will likely settle for an amount which would merely cripple the bank but not kill it as long as Guild Mortgage doesn't make too much of a scene publicly.

The most telling thing is that the government has not forbid ANY of these lending institutions from making FHA loans or doing business with the GSE's. You'd think if the banks were so bad that the government would cut them off. Even the smaller mortgage companies with no real lobbying groups are spared, provided they pay the money. For reference, any institutions today found not lending money to minorities with low credit scores WILL get cut off from the government programs.

To stay in business as a lending institution is to follow a simple formula: Give the government their money, keep making the bad loans the government wants you to make, and don't worry about being stuck with those bad loans because the government will keep forcing the GSE's to buy them. For now, business as usual. Then after the next real estate crash we'll play the same song and dance again.

The downside to all of this is that it really hurts the lower income consumers. Large companies like Quicken Loans and JP Morgan Chase are leading the charge to dump FHA loans. The banks still in the FHA game are charging higher interest rates to consumers than they otherwise would to mitigate the risk of a government shake down. Consumers now need to go under a fine tooth comb and self employed people are very limited in their lending options (unless they have over 250k in assets in the bank of course). The restrictions on pay to loan officers have created a perverse disincentive to even deal with low income borrowers.

Banks aren't saints, far from it, but this witch hunt of the big banks with regards to FHA loans in the mid-2000's is one of the many "bread and circuses" we are being treated to by our government.
